My First Experience with Coding

By Iqra Mukhtar2 min read

My first experience with coding was exciting but a little confusing. At first, all the code looked like a bunch of random words, symbols, and numbers, and I didn't really understand how everything worked together. But as I started learning, things slowly began to make sense.

The first time it worked

I still remember writing my first HTML code and seeing my own text appear on a webpage. It might sound like a small thing, but seeing something I created with code actually work felt really satisfying. It made me curious about what else I could create if I kept learning.

Four languages, four jobs

As I started exploring HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and C++, I realized that coding is not just about writing lines of code. HTML helps me structure a webpage, CSS makes it look better, and JavaScript adds interactivity and makes websites more dynamic. C++ has also helped me understand programming logic and problem-solving.

When the code doesn’t work

Of course, learning isn't always easy. Sometimes, even a small mistake can be frustrating, especially when the code doesn't work the way I expected. But fixing those mistakes helps me understand things better and gives me more confidence to try again.

Where I am now

I'm still a beginner, and I know I have a lot to learn. I'm looking forward to building my own websites, working on creative projects, and turning my ideas into something real.

Everyone starts somewhere.

I may be a beginner today, but everyone starts somewhere. My first experience with coding has taught me that learning takes time, patience, and practice. This is just the beginning of my journey, and I'm excited to see how far I can go with it.

The Difference Between AI and Human Illusion

By Iqra Mukhtar5 min read

Have you ever felt that an AI truly understands you? The pause, the empathy, the perfectly timed response it can feel almost human. Sometimes, an AI conversation can even feel more comforting than talking to a real person. But is the AI actually understanding you, or is your brain instinctively assigning emotion to something that only knows how to predict words?

What if the chatbot isn’t pretending to understand you and you’re the one pretending it does?

Where the illusion starts

This is where human illusion comes in, the brain’s tendency to misinterpret reality through emotions, memories, expectations, and beliefs. AI and human illusions are very different phenomena, yet they intersect in fascinating ways. We live in a world where AI has become a part of our everyday life. It is everywhere, no matter how small or big our problem might be we often turn to AI for solutions and consider it a reliable source of help. With advancements in AI, conversation has become more emotionally expressive. It behaves, converses, and responds like a human, which has led many people to believe that it has perception and emotions. This raises an interesting question.

What is the difference between AI and human illusion?

We see minds everywhere

They are very different concepts at their core but at first glance, they may seem connected. The conversations we have with AI often feel like we are talking to a person who knows us very well that’s because human beings are naturally wired to search for meaning, emotion, and connection. We project feelings onto pets, fictional characters, and even inanimate objects because humans tend to get attached to things and often search for personality in them, this is a psychological tendency called anthropomorphism assigning characteristics to non-human objects. Some examples are, talking to pets as if they’re human, or talking to your car or thinking a doll has feelings. Even though these objects are not conscious, humans emotionally react to them as if they are. This becomes especially important with AI because AI communicates using human language. When computers interact in a manner similar to that of humans we naturally believe that AI understands me emotionally and cares about me or that it has feelings, the ELIZA effect is one of the prime examples of this.

ELIZA was one of the earliest chatbots ever created. Even though it was extremely simple, many people emotionally connected with it and believed it truly understood them. This revealed something important about human psychology that how easily humans attribute understanding and emotion to machines, even when the system is following simple scripted rules.

What an AI is actually doing

AI strictly follows the rules of an LLM (Large Language Model) it is a type of artificial intelligence trained on massive amounts of text data such as books, articles, websites, and conversations. Its purpose is to understand and generate human-like language. LLMs work by using pattern recognition. Instead of truly “thinking” or understanding like humans do, they analyze patterns in language and predict the most likely next word in a sentence.

AI lacks true understanding it has been designed to respond in ways that appear helpful, agreeable, and emotionally aware, even when it does not genuinely comprehend the meaning behind the conversation. AI does not feel, or possess consciousness. Instead, it operates through pattern recognition, analyzing enormous amounts of data and predicting the most statistically likely next word based on patterns learned from human language. When an AI says “I understand how you feel,” it is not experiencing empathy the way a human does it is generating a response that resembles empathy because similar phrases frequently appeared in its training data. In this sense, AI does not truly “know” you, it follows patterns from its database and training to simulate understanding. The illusion becomes powerful because humans naturally interpret fluent language and emotional responses as signs of genuine awareness. While AI can imitate compassion, support, and conversation with remarkable accuracy, its responses are ultimately the result of algorithms processing data rather than real emotions, personal experiences, or conscious thought.

Ironically, one of the greatest illusions today may not be AI itself, but the human tendency to believe that highly realistic and emotional conversations automatically imply true understanding. As AI systems become more advanced and human-like, the real challenge may not be whether machines can think like us, but whether humans can resist the illusion that they already do.

Why talking to a machine feels safe

Many people have shared thoughts with a chatbot that they have never told another person. The important question is not whether the AI truly understood them, but why speaking to a machine felt safer than speaking to another human being. One of the most appealing qualities of AI is that it does not judge. It does not complain, mock, interrupt, or make people feel inferior. Instead, it responds with patience, reassurance, and consistency. Because of this, many individuals feel more comfortable opening up to a chatbot about their fears, emotions, and personal struggles.

Even when we know AI is only a machine, we still find comfort in these interactions because humans need validation. In many ways, the illusion is not simply that AI understands us, but that we are willing to emotionally connect with something we know is incapable of true understanding. This reveals something deeply human our desire to be heard, accepted, and understood, even if the understanding itself may only be imitation.

Using AI responsibly

At the same time, we need to understand the importance of using AI responsibly. While AI can be helpful for learning, productivity, emotional support, and communication, it should not completely replace genuine human relationships or professional help. AI can provide comfort and conversation, but it cannot truly understand human emotions, make moral judgments, or offer the depth of care that comes from real human connection and lived experience. Relying too deeply on AI may blur the line between simulated understanding and genuine empathy. As technology continues to evolve, people must learn to use AI as a tool rather than treat it as a substitute for human interaction. Responsible use of AI means recognizing both its strengths and its limitations appreciating its ability to assist us while remaining aware that behind every response is a system built on data, algorithms, and pattern recognition, not consciousness or emotion.

What's in My Kitchen?

Tell it what's in your kitchen and it finds recipes you can cook with it. Prototype, built with AI.

Try it: tap the ingredients you have

Pick a cuisine

Recipes you can make

What the app does

  • Pick ingredients from 10 categories, from vegetables and dairy to spices and canned foods, or add your own.
  • Mark ingredients that are about to expire and find recipes that use them up.
  • Choose a cuisine: Desi, Western, Italian, Korean, Japanese, Mexican or Healthy.
  • Recipes are ranked by how few ingredients you're missing, with filters for time, spice level and budget.
  • Step-by-step cooking view, favorite recipes and a shopping list.
  • Sign-in, so your kitchen is saved to your account.

Built with

React TypeScript Vite Tailwind CSS Express tRPC Drizzle + MySQL Framer Motion

The demo above uses 10 of the app's real recipes. The full app runs separately and needs a sign-in.
